title: Two Sum
statement_md:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.

tests.explain_on_fail: Basic case: the matching pair sits at the front of the array.
Half the target appears only once, so an element must never be paired with itself.
Duplicate values: two equal numbers at different indices form the pair.
The pair sits in the middle of the array rather than at either end.
Every value is negative, so the target is negative too.
Two zeros must be recognised as a pair that sums to 0.
Values at the extremes of the allowed range cancel out.
Two equal values in the middle of the array form the answer.
A maximum-size input (10^4 values) with the pair far apart — an O(n²) double loop is likely to time out.

editorial_md:
### Intuition
For every value `x`, the only number that completes the pair is `target - x`. Instead of searching for it with a second loop, remember every value you've already passed in a hash map from value to index.

### Algorithm
Walk the array once. At index `i`, check whether `target - nums[i]` is already in the map. If it is, return the stored index together with `i`. Otherwise store `nums[i] → i` and keep going.

Checking *before* inserting is what stops an element from pairing with itself.

```python
def twoSum(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []
```

### Complexity
O(n) time and O(n) extra space. The brute-force double loop is O(n²) and times out on the largest inputs.

### Alternative
Sort the indices by value and move two pointers inward from both ends — O(n log n) time, useful when you can't afford a hash map.

hints.body_md: For a given number `x`, exactly one other value can complete the pair. What is it?
The partner of `x` is `target - x`. A hash map lets you ask "have I already seen that value, and where?" in O(1), so a single pass is enough.

```
seen = empty map
for i, x in nums:
    if (target - x) in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]
    seen[x] = i
```
The key line is the lookup that happens *before* storing the current value: `if target - x in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]`.
